1:
The law is delivered not to the people but to the heads of the tribes, and Gill and Henry both explain why. Gill says the princes could more easily be convened and that it lay on them to see such laws executed; Henry adds that they were to instruct those under their charge, explain the law, give the necessary cautions and call men to account for a broken vow, and guesses that they had consulted Moses on some emergency of this kind. Clarke sorts the vows into kinds: of abstinence or humiliation, of the Nazarite, of giving things or sacrifices to the Lord, and of alms to the poor. Keil makes the division sharper and lexical. The first word is a positive vow, a promise to give or sanctify some part of one's property; the second comes from a root meaning to bind or fetter and is the negative vow, an abstinence taken upon the soul. What the abstinence consisted in is never explained, he notes, because traditional custom made it plain, and it probably meant fasting and similar refusals; he adds that the Nazarite's vow is named by the first word and not the second.

On what may be vowed the witnesses agree and give the same limits. Gill requires that the matter tend to the glory of God, the honour of religion, the service of the sanctuary or the good of a man or his neighbour, or else be simply indifferent, and reports Jarchi's rule that a man may bar himself from what is already barred and may bar what is free, but may not licence what Scripture prohibits. Henry reaches the same limit differently: no promise can oblige a man to what the precept already forbids, and the thing sworn must not have been a necessary duty beforehand — sacrifices at set times, a sum in alms, abstinence from meats the law allowed, a fast on days besides the day of atonement. Then he takes up the phrase that gives the chapter its shape. To vow is to bind the soul with a bond, and since the vow is made to God, who is a spirit, it is the soul with all its powers that is bound: a promise to a man is a bond upon the estate, but a promise to God is a bond upon the soul. He notes that the Jewish doctors called vows the hedge of separation, a fence about religion.

The obligation is absolute, and then immediately qualified. Henry presses the first: a man shall not break his word though he afterwards change his mind, and the margin's reading, that he shall not profane it, makes vowing an ordinance which hypocrisy desecrates. Better not to promise at all than to promise and not pay, since God's word to us is yea and amen and ours to him must not be yea and nay. Clarke values the law for both effects at once, that it prevented and annulled rash vows while giving a sanction to those rationally made, and thinks it must have been a great preventive of lying and hypocrisy. Calvin explains the order of the argument: the general rule is restated first so that no one should suppose the exception contradicts it, standing good but reaching only those who are their own masters; and the preface, he insists, covers lawful undertakings only, since unless what we offer pleases God it binds no conscience at all. He then raises the case the chapter passes over. Sons go unmentioned though their condition is the same, and he wonders whether God meant to regard the weaker sex; boys of ten, he conjectures, are held to what they promise, but he declines to contend for it, thinking it better to leave the doubtful undecided. Gill answers from the rabbis instead, giving thirteen years from the Targum and twelve from the Mishnah.
3:
Ellicott counts four cases in what follows: the unmarried girl in her father's house, the woman already under a pledge when she marries, the widow or divorced woman, and the wife; and he reads the whole as an enforcement of the fifth commandment. Keil takes the first case and states the principle it establishes, that obedience to a parent stood higher than a self-imposed act of religion, so that where the father held his daughter back the Lord forgave her on account of his refusal. On her age the accounts vary. Clarke gives the rabbinic reckoning, under twelve for a girl and under thirteen for a young man, and adds the reason: persons of that age were under authority and had no power to give away what belonged to another, a wife standing in the same case. Gill cites the Targum for thirteen. Henry begins further back, taking it for granted that anyone at his own disposal and of sound mind must perform whatever lawful thing he has promised, so the daughter is the exception rather than the rule; her undertaking hangs in suspense until her father learns of it, and from her, and only then may he confirm or quash it.

Silence decides it, and every witness stops on that. Henry gives the maxim that he who says nothing is taken to consent, and reads the father's quiet as allowing his daughter the liberty she has assumed. Calvin draws a wider moral: no one in authority does his duty unless he frankly and discreetly says so whenever something displeases him, since connivance is a kind of tacit approval. Henry lists the reasons a father might object. The pledge may prejudice the affairs of the house, break his own arrangements, perplex the provision for his table if it concerned meats, or reach beyond what his estate will bear; and in any case it trespasses on his authority over his child. On the timing the rule is strict. Gill insists, with Aben Ezra, that the refusal fall on the very day he hears of it, not the next and still less a third or fourth, and notes it might be done on a sabbath; for a husband the Jews allowed twenty-four hours. Wesley adds the point that decides how the day is counted: it runs not from her promise but from his knowledge of it, leaving only convenient time to deliberate. Calvin makes the same limit an argument, that what has once been approved cannot afterwards be revoked.

Then comes the clause that troubles them, that the Lord shall forgive her. Ellicott takes it plainly, that she does not incur the guilt she would otherwise have earned by leaving her promise unperformed. Calvin finds a rebuke inside the pardon: Moses gently reproves the girl's thoughtlessness, since it is blameworthy to forget one's condition and shake off the yoke and commit oneself in haste; God hints she is not innocent, but removes the scruple lest she be tormented by secret remorse. Henry is gentler still: she showed good-will, and her intentions being sincere she shall be accounted better than sacrifice. He turns it into an argument for the public interest in paternal authority, since children countenanced in disobedience become in other things children of Belial. Wesley enters the necessary limit: the discharge covers only what could not be performed without invading the father's right, and no father can release a child from a promise to forsake a sin or to do a plain duty. Clarke reaches the same boundary from the other side: a rash oath was never to be kept, since, as Philo says, a man who acts unjustly on account of it adds one crime to another. On the second case Ellicott and Keil agree: it is the woman who marries while already pledged, the husband then deciding as the father would have done.
9:
The widow and the divorced woman are the one case that goes the other way: whatever they have bound themselves to stands against them. Wesley notes that this holds even though such a woman is often back in her father's house. Calvin explains why the class is named at all, lest a woman suppose that by marrying again she escapes, being no longer her own and once more under the yoke, since people often extricate themselves by just such subtle excuses. Gill takes the harder question, what happens to a woman only betrothed. Jarchi restricts the verse to a widow of an actual marriage, and the Mishnah settles the betrothed case the other way: if the father of a betrothed girl dies the power does not pass to the husband, but if the husband dies it returns to the father. Gill draws out the paradox in it. Here the father's authority is greater than the husband's; everywhere else the husband's is greater, since a husband may cancel the promise of a woman who has come of age and a father may not.

The wife's case fills the rest and turns on the same silence. Gill notes the dispute over whom the tenth verse describes, the Targum taking her for one merely betrothed and Jarchi for a married woman, which Gill thinks likelier. Wesley supplies a concrete instance of what the verse guards against: a woman promises in her husband's lifetime that when widowed she will give part of her estate to pious uses, then repents of it once widowed and persuades herself she is free because she was not free when she spoke. Not so, he says, unless her husband disallowed it then. On the phrase about afflicting the soul, Gill and Ellicott agree it means fasting and abstinence, and Gill adds that Jarchi wrongly narrows the husband's power to that alone, the case being given as illustration rather than limit. Wesley sees the point of naming it: the husband's veto reaches not only what touches his estate but what seems to touch her body only, since her body is his right. Then comes the clause they all stop at. If he has let it stand day after day and only afterwards hinders it, Wesley says the failure is reckoned to him and not to her; and Clarke warns that her life is at stake in the obligation she has laid on herself.

The closing verse gathers the whole. Gill reads it clause by clause, the statutes between a man and his wife touching what she binds herself to and he confirms or annuls, and between a father and his daughter while she is still under age and in his house; and he names the purpose plainly, to prevent imprudent and extravagant promises and the too frequent use of them, whose consequences might be bad in families. Clarke guesses that the law arose, like that about the daughters' inheritance, from some particular case that had just occurred, and then turns severe: making such promises is in almost any case a dangerous business, they seldom do good and often much evil, and a man who is not held by the standing testimony of God's word will hardly be held by an obligation he lays on his own conscience, for if God's word lacks weight with him his own will prove lighter than vanity. Calvin uses his last paragraph to correct a misreading. The words about the husband's house have been taken by some to mean a household and its master; the subject does not admit it and the words of Moses forbid it, and he is surprised that men skilled in Hebrew have not seen it.
